title: Taking Back the “Permission to Narrate”: Examining a Grassroots Organization’s Process of Supporting BIPOC Youth in Developing Counternarratives and Counterspaces as Decolonial Resistance
abstract: Decolonial scholars have conceptualized the continuation of colonial systems of oppression as “coloniality.” Central to coloniality is the use of narrative to shape discourse, which makes colonialism possible. Colonial master narratives, a force of coloniality, deny Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) the right to self-determination and restrict lived experiences as an aspect to be constructed “through the eyes of others”. In resistance against coloniality, a critical enactment of decoloniality involves BIPOC communities taking back the “permission to narrate” through “counternarratives” and “counterspaces.” Youth-focused grassroots organizations can play pivotal roles in supporting BIPOC youth in cultivating “counternarratives” and “counterspaces” as critical to decolonial and antiracism processes. This study used community-based, decolonial qualitative methods in partnership with The City School (TCS), a grassroots youth-focused organization in Boston, to explore how they support young BIPOCs’ resistance against coloniality and interrelated systems of oppression. Findings suggest that TCS acts as a decolonial counterspace in which young BIPOC can take back the power to tell their own stories, challenge colonial logics, construct identity, and resist alienation through community connection.
